evidence: createHttpServer registers Express routes (app.post/app.get/app.patch) and uses express.json(): HTTP transport, which fits infrastructure.
The checks in the route handlers (`typeof stock !== "number"`, `Array.isArray(items)`, the productId/quantity type checks) only validate the shape of request data at the transport boundary.
Every handler passes the business work to FulfilmentService (e.g. service.placeOrder, service.advanceOrder, service.cancelOrder), so no business rules live in the adapter.
The error middleware maps NotFoundError to 404, DomainError to 400 and anything else to 500. Mapping errors to HTTP statuses is a transport concern.
The `orderStates.includes(state as OrderState)` check decodes untrusted input against the domain's own list. It doesn't redefine any business rule.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
Everything in src/infrastructure/http-server.ts is inbound transport (HTTP adapter) work. That work belongs in the infrastructure layer:
- It sets up Express routes.
- It parses request bodies and query strings and checks their types and shapes.
- It turns HTTP input into application-service calls (service.addProduct, placeOrder, listOrders, getOrder, advanceOrder, cancelOrder).
- It maps errors to HTTP status codes (404 for NotFoundError, 400 for DomainError, 500 otherwise).

The file holds no business rules. It doesn't check stock, decide which state transitions are allowed, check whether an order can be cancelled, or calculate pricing. All of that is left to the application service.

The check that `state` is in `orderStates` uses the domain's own list to decode untrusted input, so it doesn't redefine any domain rule. There are two small issues, neither of which moves a responsibility into the wrong layer:
- The error message repeats the list of state names as a hardcoded string.
- Transport-level validation failures are thrown as DomainError instead of a transport-specific error type.
